articles.title: A city of “ambiguous loss”: digital methods and a multiscalar examination of Jewish Budapest in the aftermath of the Holocaust
articles.authors: Cole, Tim; Giordano, Alberto; Le Noc, Maël
articles.abstract: Abstract This article focuses on an understudied phenomenon in the immediate postwar period: the existence of a liminal group of Jewish men whose fate remained unknown. To identify this group in one city with a large postwar Jewish population, the article intentionally draws on mixed methods, including a traditional close reading of oral history interviews and a spatial analysis of a large-scale survey of Jewish survivors living in Budapest that was quickly undertaken by a coalition of Jewish organizations in summer 1945 and published and distributed in 1946 under the title Counted Remnant: Register of the Jewish Survivors in Budapest. This article addresses the narrow question of how what contemporary therapists dub “ambiguous loss” was experienced in one post-Holocaust city, as well as two broader issues. First, it signals that the postwar context was more complex than the binary of returning Jewish survivors (the names listed in Counted Remnant) and non-returning Jewish victims who had been murdered (the names not listed in Counted Remnant). Rather, by adopting a method dubbed distant reading “against the grain,” this study identifies the existence of a third, large group of Hungarian Jewish men who neither were dead nor had returned home in the postwar years. Second, by intentionally adopting a range of methods that include both distant and close reading, this article explores the value in adopting mixed-method approaches, including from the digital humanities—alongside multiscalar geographical analysis—within “integrated” histories and geographies of the Holocaust.
